_comment: FROZEN golden wire vectors for the claim/hold-query surface (daemon/src/claim.rs). Filed by task-91, which ADDS the batched hold-query alongside these types: the freeze on HoldQuery/HoldAnswer/HoldResponse/Claim was stated in prose and enforced only by round-trip tests, which pass just as happily after a field is renamed on both sides. These vectors pin the exact BYTES, so a change to the frozen encodings fails here instead of splitting the network silently. Changing any `wire` string is a deliberate, reviewed re-freeze that requires a `schema_version` bump. `daemon/tests/claim_wire_golden.rs` asserts each `wire` is what our encoder EMITS and what our decoder ACCEPTS.
_direction: Each vector declares a `direction`. `both` = our encoder must EMIT exactly these bytes AND our decoder must ACCEPT them. `decode-only` = a legal input we must keep ACCEPTING but do not emit (an omitted defaulted field, a dropped unknown kind). The second class exists because an encoding vector is blind to a change in what we TOLERATE: adding `skip_serializing_if`, or removing `serde(default)`, left every pre-existing vector in this file green. `reject` = a wire we must REFUSE. That class exists because the file pinned emitted bytes well and had NO way to say "this must not decode", so every acceptance-widening change passed by construction: removing `deny_unknown_fields` from BatchHoldQuery, or from a KnownTransport, left every vector green.
codec: JSON draft codec (claim.rs `Codec` note): the field order is the struct declaration order, so the byte string is stable. The final binary codec is a velocity surface and will re-pin these vectors under a new file.

identities._note: The exact canonical strings the vectors are built from. The test asserts its own typed constructors produce these, so a vector can never be pinned against an identity encoding that has itself drifted.

vectors.name: claim_full
vectors.note: A fully-populated v1 claim: known payload (the ONE content identity), both holders, both transports. `relay`/`signatures` are absent from the wire because they are None/empty in v1.

vectors.name: claim_v2_reserved_fields
vectors.note: The RESERVED v2 fields, POPULATED. `claim_full` leaves relay=None/signatures=[], which means their field names were unpinned - `relay.blob`, `signatures[].key_id` and `signatures[].sig` could all be renamed with every golden test still green. Those fields exist precisely so that v2 needs no wire break, so their names are part of the freeze and are pinned here.

vectors.name: claim_transports_omitted
vectors.note: ACCEPTED LEGACY INPUT: a claim with no `transports` field at all decodes to an empty offer set (`serde(default)`). Pinning what we ACCEPT is a separate obligation from pinning what we emit: removing the `default` would keep every encoding vector green while making this legal wire un-decodable.

vectors.name: claim_unknown_transport_dropped
vectors.note: ACCEPTED LEGACY INPUT: an unknown transport KIND between two known ones is TOLERATED and DROPPED (never carried, never re-serialised), while the known ones survive in order. This is the rule that lets a future transport ship without a network fork, so it is pinned on bytes.

vectors.name: hold_query
vectors.note: The single-key probe. task-91 adds a BATCHED query alongside it; this vector is what proves the single-key form was not mutated in the process.

vectors.name: hold_response_have
vectors.note: `answer` is FLATTENED into the envelope, so the tag sits next to schema_version. The blake3 appears exactly once; the offer is a pure locator.

vectors.name: hold_response_have_empty_offers
vectors.note: A Have with an EMPTY offer list, which is legal and reachable (a holder whose only locator kind this build cannot express). It is pinned because the non-empty vector above cannot see a `skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty"` being added: that mutation changes THESE bytes to `{..."blake3":...}` and nothing else. It survived the whole golden suite before this vector existed.

vectors.name: hold_response_have_offers_omitted
vectors.note: ACCEPTED LEGACY INPUT: `offers` omitted entirely decodes to an empty offer set. Pins the DECODER's tolerance, which no encoding vector can see - removing `serde(default)` leaves every emitted byte identical and silently stops accepting this wire.

vectors.name: hold_response_absent
vectors.note: A no. It carries no blake3 and no offers - there is nothing on this wire that could enumerate what the peer DOES hold.

vectors.name: batch_hold_query
vectors.note: task-91 ADDITION. The same question as `hold_query`, asked about many keys at once. The keys are the asker's own, in the asker's own order, and that order is what the answer vector is aligned to.

vectors.name: batch_hold_response
vectors.note: task-91 ADDITION. One positional answer per queried key. The offers form a DICTIONARY and each Have names its own by INDEX - here one peer-scoped iroh locator shared by both Haves, which is the common case and the reason the dictionary exists (256 keys cost one copy of the locator, not 256). NOTE WHAT IS ABSENT: no `sha256:` string appears anywhere on this wire.

vectors.name: batch_hold_response_all_absent
vectors.note: task-91 ADDITION. An all-absent answer MUST carry an empty dictionary: an offer no answer references is rejected by the codec, so a peer cannot attach a content-specific locator to a response that answered nothing. The empty `offers` is emitted, not omitted - one canonical form.

vectors.name: batch_hold_response_distinct_locators
vectors.note: task-91 ADDITION, and the regression vector for the defect that sent this task back: two keys, each with its OWN content-specific BitTorrent infohash, sharing one peer-scoped iroh locator. Under the earlier response-wide offer list this was inexpressible and key 2's claim silently received key 1's infohash.

vectors.name: batch_hold_response_unknown_transport_slot
vectors.note: ACCEPTED INPUT, and the subtlest rule in this file: an unknown transport kind is tolerated-but-dropped, but the offers are INDEXED, so dropping element 1 in place would rebind the second Have's index 2 onto the wrong locator. The decoder keeps a SLOT for every element the peer sent, validates the indices against those RAW positions, then compacts and REWRITES the indices together. Note the unknown slot IS referenced (by answer 0) - it has to be, because an offer no answer references is rejected - so this also pins that dropping it leaves answer 0 with a SHORTER index list rather than a dangling one. Must decode to offers [iroh, bittorrent] with the Haves naming [0] and [1].

vectors.name: batch_hold_response_have_empty_offer_indices
vectors.note: A `Have` with an EMPTY `offer_indices`: legal and reachable (a holder whose only locators were unknown transport kinds, which are dropped on decode). Pinned because no other vector has one - so `skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty"` added to `offer_indices` changed THESE bytes and nothing else, exactly the hole that the `offers` field had before an empty-offers vector existed.

vectors.name: reject_claim_known_transport_with_stray_blake3
vectors.note: MUST REJECT. A KNOWN `iroh` transport carrying a second identity-like field. This DECODED before round 7 - the stray was ignored because the typed offer has no digest field - so the bytes carried two identity-like values and were accepted. That is a property of this build, not of the wire: another implementation could read it differently. `KnownTransport` is `deny_unknown_fields` now.

vectors.name: reject_claim_known_payload_with_unknown_field
vectors.note: MUST REJECT. A KNOWN `whole_nar` payload with an extra field. Same rule as the transport above, one level up: a kind we DO understand must mean exactly what we think it means.

vectors.name: reject_batch_hold_query_unknown_field
vectors.note: MUST REJECT. `BatchHoldQuery` carries `deny_unknown_fields`, and NOTHING asserted it: removing the attribute left the whole suite green. An encoding vector cannot see a decoder becoming more permissive, which is what this whole vector class is for.

vectors.name: reject_batch_response_offer_bound_to_no_answer
vectors.note: MUST REJECT. An all-`Absent` answer set with a non-empty offer dictionary: a locator bound to no answered key. This is the no-enumeration half of the offer-hoisting defect, pinned on BYTES rather than only in a unit test.

vectors.name: reject_batch_response_two_locators_of_one_kind
vectors.note: MUST REJECT. One answer naming TWO `bittorrent` offers. The content behind a key has ONE identity per transport, so the second names a different blob. This is the rule that bounds the dictionary against ANSWERED keys; without it a single `Have` could legitimise all 512 entries.

vectors.name: reject_batch_answer_absent_with_a_field
vectors.note: MUST REJECT. An `Absent` answer carrying a content identity. `Absent` is an empty STRUCT variant precisely so `deny_unknown_fields` bites; as a UNIT variant the attribute was silently inert and this wire decoded.

vectors.name: reject_hold_response_two_locators_of_one_kind
vectors.note: MUST REJECT (task-110). A SINGLE-KEY `Have` naming TWO `iroh` offers. The frozen single-key path had no offer count cap at all - 622 offers = 65,440 B against an 88 B query = 743.6x, and a bittorrent infohash is a content identity, so this was also a no-enumeration vector. The DELIBERATE freeze amendment (see claim.rs `check_single_offer_bindings`) bounds a one-key `Have` to one offer per transport kind, the same theorem the batch path uses. This closes the KNOWN-offer count/enumeration vector (<=1 KNOWN content identity per transport kind, consistent with deny_unknown_fields). The unknown-KIND enumeration's STRUCTURAL/list half is closed separately by TASK-224 (see reject_hold_response_unknown_transport_names_content_ids). ONE residual remains DISTINCT from this count bound and shared with the batch path: the identity-shaped TEXT residual (a single string via tag/field-name/value, TASK-227). The worst-case BYTE amplification (a well-shaped unknown-kind offer's single scalar was byte-unbounded, so a hostile Have could pad to the 64 KiB frame) has since been CLOSED by the per-offer byte cap (TASK-223, see reject_hold_response_offer_over_byte_cap and claim.rs MAX_OFFER_WIRE_BYTES). Pinned on BYTES so the narrowing is auditable here, not only in a unit test.

vectors.name: reject_hold_response_unknown_transport_names_content_ids
vectors.note: MUST REJECT (task-224, single-key path). An UNKNOWN transport KIND whose body carries a `content_ids` ARRAY of two blake3 digests. Before task-224 the tolerate-drop decoder read only the `transport` tag and accepted-then-dropped the rest as an opaque value, so this wire NAMED two content identities the asker never queried and was ACCEPTED - the exact `also_held` enumeration case deny_unknown_fields forecloses for a KNOWN transport, on the unknown-KIND path. The DELIBERATE freeze amendment (see claim.rs `reject_enumeration_shaped_unknown_offer`) constrains a tolerated unknown-kind offer to the `transport` tag plus AT MOST one scalar string locator; an array, a nested object, or a second field is REJECTED, not dropped, because accepting-then-dropping a wire that named identities is itself the defect. A well-shaped unknown offer (tag + one scalar) still decodes inertly (forward-compat, see claim_unknown_transport_dropped). Pinned on BYTES so the narrowing is auditable here.

vectors.name: reject_batch_response_unknown_transport_names_content_ids
vectors.note: MUST REJECT (task-224, batch path). The SAME enumeration-shaped unknown-kind offer as reject_hold_response_unknown_transport_names_content_ids, referenced by one positional Have. The single-key and batch decoders share `deserialize_transport_slots`, so this pins that the STRUCTURAL/list closure is identical on both paths - a hostile peer cannot smuggle a LIST of content identities (array/nested/multi-field) in an accepted-then-dropped slot on either. NOT literal closure: a single identity-shaped string can still ride via the tag, an extra field name, or the value (TEXT residual, TASK-227 - distinct from TASK-223, which is byte VOLUME only).

vectors.name: reject_claim_unknown_transport_names_content_ids
vectors.note: MUST REJECT (task-224, claim path). The same enumeration-shaped unknown-kind offer inside a Claim's `transports` list. `deserialize_known_transports` (the claim twin of `deserialize_transport_slots`) shares the shape rule, so the freeze amendment closes the STRUCTURAL/list vector on the claim path too; the two are kept in step by claim.rs `the_slot_and_drop_transport_decoders_agree`. A well-shaped unknown transport in a claim still decodes inertly (see claim_unknown_transport_dropped); the identity-shaped TEXT residual (single string via tag/field-name/value) remains, owned by TASK-227.

vectors.name: reject_hold_response_unknown_transport_non_string_tag
vectors.note: MUST REJECT (task-224 strict-allowlist tightening). An unknown offer whose `transport` tag is a NUMBER, not a string. The old decoder mapped an absent/non-string tag to an empty tag and ACCEPTED the offer (dropping it), so a non-string tag was itself a smuggling channel. A tolerated unknown kind must now POSITIVELY declare a string `transport`; absent/null/number/boolean/array/object tags are refused. Pins the string-tag clause on bytes so a selective weakening bites.

vectors.name: reject_hold_response_offer_over_byte_cap
vectors.note: MUST REJECT (task-223, single-key path). A well-shaped unknown-kind offer (tag + ONE scalar string `loc`, admitted by task-224) whose single scalar pads the offer past the MAX_OFFER_WIRE_BYTES=2 KiB per-offer cap. Before task-223 the count/kind + shape rules were a COUNT/STRUCTURE bound, not a BYTE bound, so a single fat offer could pad a one-key `Have` toward the 64 KiB frame (~744x) and was ACCEPTED-then-dropped. The DELIBERATE freeze amendment (see claim.rs `offer_within_byte_cap` / `MAX_OFFER_WIRE_BYTES`) now REFUSES any offer whose serialized size exceeds the cap, so one offer can no longer fill the frame. The cap is deliberately GENEROUS over any plausible legit locator (loosening later is backward-safe); a well-shaped UNDER-cap unknown offer still decodes inertly (see claim_unknown_transport_dropped). Pinned on BYTES so the narrowing is auditable here.

vectors.name: reject_batch_response_offer_over_byte_cap
vectors.note: MUST REJECT (task-223, batch path). The SAME over-cap unknown-kind offer as reject_hold_response_offer_over_byte_cap, referenced by one positional Have. The single-key and batch decoders share `deserialize_transport_slots` / `offer_within_byte_cap`, so this pins that the per-offer byte cap is identical on both paths - a hostile peer cannot pad a one-answer batch response to the frame with one fat offer either.

vectors.name: reject_claim_offer_over_byte_cap
vectors.note: MUST REJECT (task-223, claim path). The same over-cap unknown-kind offer inside a Claim's `transports` list. `deserialize_known_transports` (the claim twin) shares `offer_within_byte_cap`, so the per-offer byte cap holds on the claim path too; the two are kept in step by claim.rs `the_slot_and_drop_transport_decoders_agree`.
